articles.title: China’s Tianwen-1 captures interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS near Mars
articles.summary: China’s Tianwen-1 orbiter captured a faint but remarkable view of 3I/ATLAS as the interstellar comet raced past Mars. The images reveal its tail and glowing coma, offering scientists a glimpse of material born beyond our solar system.
articles.content:
China's Tianwen-1 spacecraft has photographed the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS as it passed near Mars. According to the China National Space Agency (CNSA), the orbiter used its high-resolution camera to capture the comet from about 30 million km (18.6 million mi) away.

Tianwen-1 has been orbiting Mars for four years and eight months, making it one of the closest spacecraft to observe the interstellar object since its discovery (on May 7th, 2025).

Tianwen-1 Reveals the Comet's Tail and Coma

The new images show several features that support the conclusion that 3I/ATLAS is a comet. A visible tail extends behind the object, while a cloud of gas and dust (coma) surrounds its nucleus.

Researchers combined multiple images into an animation that traces the comet's movement as it travels toward its closest approach to the Sun. The observations add to growing evidence that 3I/ATLAS contains water and other volatile materials that began escaping as the object warmed during its journey through the inner solar system.

The successful observation also provides a preview of the type of work China hopes to conduct with Tianwen-2. That mission is expected to visit a Near Earth Asteroid (NEA) and later study a comet.

Capturing a Small and Fast-Moving Target

The team responsible for Tianwen-1's High-Resolution Imaging Camera (HiRIC) began preparing for the encounter in early September. Their work included repeated simulations, theoretical modeling, and detailed inspections of the instrument.

Photographing 3I/ATLAS was difficult because the object was both distant and relatively small (5.6 km, 3.5 mi in diameter). Its speed added another major challenge. The comet was moving at around 58 km/s (36 mi/s), while its motion relative to Tianwen-1 reached approximately 86 km/s (53.5 mi/s).

The camera also was not originally built to observe such a dim object. HiRIC was designed primarily to study bright features on the Martian surface, much like instruments aboard the European Space Agency's Mars Express and ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft.

Mars Orbiters Turn Their Cameras Toward 3I/ATLAS

On October 3rd, both European orbiters also photographed 3I/ATLAS. Mars Express used its High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC), while the ExoMars spacecraft relied on its Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS).

The comet was exceptionally difficult to detect with these instruments. When compared with sunlit features on Mars, 3I/ATLAS appeared roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times fainter.

The High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) aboard Mars Express uses an exposure time of 0.5 seconds, while the Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS) can expose an image for 5 seconds. Tianwen-1 collected its observations with the High-Resolution Imaging Camera (HiRIC).

Although HiRIC's exposure time has not been released publicly, the camera was engineered for precise timing and rapid operation. Those capabilities allowed the team to obtain the latest image, even though it appears (albeit grainy and blurry).

A Rare Sample From Another Star System

Like the two interstellar objects identified before it, 3I/ATLAS offers unusual opportunities for both astronomy and astrobiology. Asteroids and comets preserve leftover material from the formation of planetary systems, so an object arriving from interstellar space may contain clues about conditions around another star.

Studying such a visitor could reveal how other planetary systems formed and what kinds of materials they contain. A mission designed to intercept an interstellar object (for which numerous concepts are being explored) could gather information that scientists cannot obtain through ordinary telescopic observations.

The only comparable alternative would involve sending spacecraft directly to another star, an undertaking that would require enormous amounts of time and money.

Future Missions Could Chase Interstellar Visitors

Scientists hope that future spacecraft will be prepared to intercept newly discovered interstellar objects and examine them at close range.

One effort already under development is the European Space Agency's Comet Interceptor. The mission is expected to be completed by 2029 and will wait in space for an opportunity to investigate a suitable comet or other promising target.

articles.personality_title: China’s Tianwen-1 captures rare images of interstellar comet near Mars
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Tianwen-1 is a Chinese spacecraft orbiting Mars for nearly five years. Recently, scientists discovered a rare comet called 3I/ATLAS that came from outside our solar system and passed close to Mars.

**What happened** – In early October 2025, Tianwen-1 used its high-resolution camera to take pictures of 3I/ATLAS from about 30 million kilometers away. The images show the comet’s glowing coma and long tail, confirming it is a comet made of gas, dust, and ice. The comet moves very fast, making it hard to capture.

**Impact** – These photos give scientists a rare chance to study materials from another star system. Because comets hold clues about how planets form, 3I/ATLAS helps us learn about conditions far beyond Earth’s neighborhood. The success also shows how China’s space missions are improving, preparing for future studies of asteroids and comets.

**What's next step** – China plans a new mission called Tianwen-2 to visit asteroids and comets closer to Earth. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency is building a spacecraft called Comet Interceptor, set to launch by 2029 to study interstellar objects like 3I/ATLAS up close.

**One-sentence takeaway** – China’s Tianwen-1 has captured important images of a fast-moving comet from another star system, opening new paths to explore space beyond our solar system.
articles.personality_title_fr: Tianwen-1 de Chine capture des images rares d'une comète interstellaire près de Mars
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Tianwen-1 est un engin spatial chinois en orbite autour de Mars depuis presque cinq ans. Récemment, les scientifiques ont découvert une comète rare appelée 3I/ATLAS venue de l'extérieur de notre système solaire, passant près de Mars.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Début octobre 2025, Tianwen-1 a utilisé sa caméra haute résolution pour prendre des photos de 3I/ATLAS à environ 30 millions de kilomètres. Les images montrent la coma brillante et la longue queue de la comète, confirmant qu'il s'agit d'une comète faite de gaz, poussière et glace. La comète se déplace très vite, ce qui rend la capture difficile.

**Impact** – Ces photos offrent aux scientifiques une chance rare d’étudier des matériaux venus d’un autre système stellaire. Comme les comètes gardent des indices sur la formation des planètes, 3I/ATLAS aide à mieux comprendre les conditions loin de notre voisinage terrestre. Ce succès montre aussi les progrès des missions spatiales chinoises, qui préparent des études futures d’astéroïdes et de comètes.

**Prochaine étape** – La Chine prévoit une nouvelle mission, Tianwen-2, pour visiter des astéroïdes et des comètes proches de la Terre. Par ailleurs, l’Agence spatiale européenne construit un engin appelé Comet Interceptor, prévu pour 2029, qui étudiera de près des objets interstellaires comme 3I/ATLAS.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Tianwen-1 de Chine a capturé des images importantes d’une comète rapide venue d’un autre système stellaire, ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour explorer l’espace au-delà de notre système solaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Tianwen-1 de China captura imágenes raras de un cometa interestelar cerca de Marte
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Tianwen-1 es una nave espacial china que orbita Marte desde hace casi cinco años. Recientemente, los científicos descubrieron un cometa raro llamado 3I/ATLAS que vino de fuera de nuestro sistema solar y pasó cerca de Marte.

**Qué pasó** – A principios de octubre de 2025, Tianwen-1 usó su cámara de alta resolución para tomar fotos de 3I/ATLAS desde unos 30 millones de kilómetros. Las imágenes muestran la coma brillante y la larga cola del cometa, confirmando que es un cometa hecho de gas, polvo y hielo. El cometa se mueve muy rápido, lo que hace difícil capturarlo.

**Impacto** – Estas fotos dan a los científicos una oportunidad rara para estudiar materiales de otro sistema estelar. Como los cometas guardan pistas sobre cómo se forman los planetas, 3I/ATLAS ayuda a entender mejor las condiciones lejos del vecindario terrestre. El éxito también muestra cómo mejoran las misiones espaciales chinas, preparándose para futuros estudios de asteroides y cometas.

**Próximo paso** – China planea una nueva misión llamada Tianwen-2 para visitar asteroides y cometas cercanos a la Tierra. Mientras tanto, la Agencia Espacial Europea está construyendo una nave llamada Comet Interceptor, que se lanzará en 2029 para estudiar objetos interestelares como 3I/ATLAS de cerca.

**Resumen en una frase** – Tianwen-1 de China ha capturado imágenes importantes de un cometa rápido de otro sistema estelar, abriendo nuevos caminos para explorar el espacio más allá de nuestro sistema solar.
